prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: Operating and Financial Metrics (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Metric" · longest unbreakable word 92px · one-line width 452px
  col 2: header "FY 2022" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 67px
  col 3: header "FY 2023" · longest unbreakable word 69px · one-line width 69px
  col 4: header "FY 2024" · longest unbreakable word 64px · one-line width 68px
  col 5: header "Q1 2025" · longest unbreakable word 70px · one-line width 70px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 557px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 556px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"good","why":"Headers and all figures sit on one line, numeric columns are evenly sized and the metric column is readable; however it spends a little too much width on the numeric columns (lots of empty space right of the short figures), so 'Net revenue retention, trailing twelve months' breaks into three lines with a weak orphan ('twelve months')."},"B":{"grade":"bad","why":"Metric column is squeezed to ~90px: rows run five to six lines and one label literally breaks mid-word ('percentag / e of revenue'), which is unacceptable for a publication table. Meanwhile the four numeric columns are far wider than their content needs, leaving big dead zones beside the numbers — space badly misallocated."},"C":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Metric column is generously sized so labels break sensibly (max three lines), and figures are intact, but 'FY 2024' wraps to two lines while the neighbouring year headers stay on one, breaking the parallel header series and making the header band ragged; the FY 2024 column also reads as slightly narrower than its siblings."},"D":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Best balance: all four period headers and every figure sit on one line, the metric column takes the remaining width and wraps into two to four tidy lines ('Net revenue retention, / trailing twelve months'), so the row-header hierarchy is clear, the year series is parallel, and the numeric columns are tight without clipping."},"E":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Essentially the same trade-off as C: comfortable metric column and intact figures, but 'FY 2024' is forced onto two lines, so the header row is uneven and the four year columns no longer read as an identical series; it looks near-identical to C in the render."},"F":{"grade":"good","why":"Headers and figures all on one line and the metric column is close to optimal, but the wrapping is slightly less tidy than D — first row still takes three lines and 'Sales and marketing expense as a percentage of revenue' runs to four, giving a less even row rhythm."}},"best":["D"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"I am estimating widths by eye, so A, D and F are within a few pixels of each other; C and E look practically identical in the renders, and I cannot be sure D's minimal numeric columns wouldn't clip a slightly wider figure or header in another rendering context."}
